newsitem.title: USA: Conn. watchdog warns tax receipts might fall short.
newsitem.headline: Conn. watchdog warns tax receipts might fall short.

text.p: Connecticut Comptroller Nancy Wyman urged on Tuesday that the state direct most of its $250 million surplus to its Rainy Day Fund, adding she was concerned tax receipts might fall short of the state's goals.
Wyman said higher income tax collections, which resulted from "booming" financial markets, produced the surplus and warned the state's tax projections might be overly optimistic.
"The one-time nature of these receipts may prove problematic in meeting revenue targets for the current fiscal year," the comptroller said in prepared remarks.

While advising the governor and legislature to not spend the surplus on programs that have recurring costs, she also highlighted deficiencies in accounts for Medicaid and home placement of children that total $86 million.

Gov. John Rowland, earlier said that about $160.5 million of the approximately $250 million surplus for the 1996 fiscal year would be deposited in the Rainy Day Fund, with around $89.5 million used to repay debt accumulated in 1991.
Connecticut's cumulative general fund deficit, when measured according to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), is projected at $598 million at June 30, 1996, Wyman said.

This accounting system becomes the state's official accounting system starting July 1, 1997, when the new fiscal year begins. Under the law, the GAAP deficit will begin to be amoritized over a 15-year period starting July 1, 1998.
